## (a) One-particle basis and spin-singlet states

Let f=n,p denote neutron or proton, and s=↑,↓ denote spin. Write the position of lattice site r as x_r=a r, where a=L_phy/L. With periodic boundary conditions, the allowed momenta are k=2πm/L_phy, with integer components m chosen in the first Brillouin zone. Define

f†_{k s}=L^(-3/2) Σ_r exp(i k·x_r) f†_{r s},    |k,f,s⟩=f†_{k s}|0⟩.

The four one-particle species-spin labels are n↑, n↓, p↑, and p↓. The free lattice dispersion following from the kinetic Hamiltonian is

ε_lat(k)=2t Σ_{i=x,y,z}[1−cos(k_i a)].

The spin-singlet spin wavefunction is (|↑↓⟩−|↓↑⟩)/√2. For identical flavors f=n or p, a zero-total-momentum singlet is

|ff;k,S=0⟩=[f†_{k↑}f†_{−k↓}−f†_{k↓}f†_{−k↑}]|0⟩/√2.

This gives the nn and pp states by choosing f=n or f=p. The displayed normalization applies when k and −k are distinct modulo reciprocal-lattice vectors. At a self-inverse momentum such as k=0, the normalized identical-flavor state is instead f†_{k↑}f†_{−k↓}|0⟩; for other momenta, k and −k label the same singlet and should not be counted twice.

For an ordered neutron-proton pair, assigning momentum k to the neutron gives

|np;k,S=0⟩=[n†_{k↑}p†_{−k↓}−n†_{k↓}p†_{−k↑}]|0⟩/√2.

Since neutron and proton are distinct flavors, this state is normalized as written also at k=0. If an even-parity S-wave state with definite isospin is intended, the spin-singlet channel has symmetric isospin (T=1); its T_z=0 component is the symmetric combination of the ordered np and pn assignments.

## (b) Matching t

The zero-momentum mode of the stated kinetic Hamiltonian has ε_lat(0)=0. Thus matching the literal lowest kinetic energy cannot determine t. The meaningful interpretation is to match the lowest nonzero momentum mode, with the rest energy subtracted. Its momentum is k=(2π/L_phy,0,0), or a sign/permutation thereof, and its lattice energy is

ε_lat,min=2t[1−cos(2π/L)],

where L is the number of lattice sites along each side. The corresponding nonrelativistic finite-box energy is

ε_phys,min=(2π/L_phy)^2/(2M_phy).

Equating the two yields the exact finite-lattice matching result

2t[1−cos(2π/L)]=(2π/L_phy)^2/(2M_phy),

t=π²/{M_phy L_phy²[1−cos(2π/L)]}.

Using a=L_phy/L and 1−cos(2π/L)≈2π²/L² for large L gives the continuum-spacing limit

t≈1/(2M_phy a²),    t a²→1/(2M_phy).

The lattice Hamiltonian has no rest-energy term, explaining its zero kinetic energy at k=0. At fixed physical box size, t itself diverges as a→0; the combination t a² sets the continuum kinetic term.

## (c) Lowest nonzero single-particle energy

Using ℏc=197.326 MeV·fm, the lowest nonzero momentum for L_phy=3.4 fm is

p_min=2πℏc/L_phy≈364.6 MeV.

Therefore its kinetic energy is

E_min=p_min²/(2M_phy)=(364.6 MeV)²/[2(1634 MeV)]≈40.7 MeV.

The zero-momentum kinetic energy is still zero; 40.7 MeV is the lowest nonzero energy. The exact finite-lattice matching in (b) matches this mode to the same continuum value. A numerical value of t at finite lattice spacing would additionally require the site count L.

## (d) Contact coupling and first excitation

The stated limits need care: the thermodynamic limit (physical volume tending to infinity) is not the same as the continuum limit (lattice spacing tending to zero). A three-dimensional continuum contact interaction requires ultraviolet regularization, and its bare coupling depends on the regulator. Consequently, the binding energy alone does not determine a regulator-independent numerical value of the lattice parameter C.

For example, at fixed lattice spacing set U=Ct and use dimensionless lattice momentum q in the Brillouin zone. For a zero-total-momentum pair, the free two-particle energy is 2ε(q)=4tΣ_i[1−cos(q_i)]. A bound state at energy −B obeys

1/(Ct)=−∫_[−π,π]^3 d³q/(2π)³ · 1/{B+4tΣ_i[1−cos(q_i)]}.

This makes C negative for an attractive interaction and determines its bare value once t, or equivalently the lattice spacing/cutoff, is specified. The bare C changes when the cutoff changes.

Equivalently, with a sharp spherical continuum momentum cutoff Λ, a regulated contact coupling g(Λ) satisfies

1/g(Λ)=−∫_|q|<Λ d³q/(2π)³ · 1/(B+q²/M)
       =−M/(2π²)[Λ−κ arctan(Λ/κ)],    κ=√(MB).

For B=17.8 MeV and M=1634 MeV,

κ≈170.5 MeV,    a_s=ℏc/κ≈1.16 fm.

These are physical zero-range scales, not a numerical bare lattice C. In the infinite-volume continuum at zero center-of-mass momentum, the bound state is at −17.8 MeV and scattering states have E=q²/M, forming a continuum from zero upward. Thus zero is the scattering threshold, not a discrete first-excited energy. A discrete first-excited level requires a specified finite physical volume and regulator.

## (e) Second excitation and degeneracy

In the specified infinite-volume continuum there is no discrete second-excited level or finite degeneracy to report: the scattering spectrum is continuous. A finite periodic box discretizes that spectrum, but its interacting levels and degeneracies require the box size and regulator. As an illustration only, for free zero-total-momentum relative motion, identifying q and −q gives three independent directions in the |m|²=1 shell and six in the |m|²=2 shell. These free-shell counts are not degeneracies of the infinite-volume interacting spectrum.

**Unresolved input and interpretation:** Parts (b)–(c) use the lowest nonzero kinetic mode because the literal lowest mode has zero energy. Parts (d)–(e), as stated, do not specify discrete excited levels in the thermodynamic limit; a numerical bare C also needs a lattice spacing/cutoff. Finally, taking L (the number of sites) to infinity at fixed a is distinct from taking a→0 at fixed physical box size.
